subject: Fuaran-Core
$comment: What the proof leg COSTS, declared per module, so that a growth in prover time is named rather than discovered when CI times out. `proofs/check.ps1` reads this file: every green CHECK line prints the module's measured seconds beside its budget, and a run over budget prints a named COST warning — never a failure on its own, because prover time varies by machine and by load and a budget is a smoke detector rather than a gate. `check.ps1 -Strict` promotes the warnings to a red leg for a session that wants one. This is NOT `proofs.json`: that file is the claims ladder — what is proved, tested and assumed, at a closed set of levels, checked row-by-row against the tree by the Proofs.Ladder family — and a wall-clock budget is a claim at none of those levels and is not per-claim but per-module. The ladder's `proof-leg` policy row points here for the cost half. Coverage is checked BOTH ways: a module the leg checks with no entry here, and an entry here for a module the leg does not check, are each a COST warning naming what to do. Hand-authored; the seeding rule below says how a number is arrived at, and bumping one is the recorded act the README's `Running it` section describes.

seeding.rule: budgetSeconds = max(2 x the slowest observed cold-cache run, 20s), rounded up to the next 10s.
seeding.$comment: The tolerance is applied ONCE, here, when a number is seeded — `check.ps1` multiplies nothing, so the pair it prints is the measurement against the ceiling and there is no second arithmetic to hold in your head. Seeded from the SLOWEST observed cold run rather than the median, deliberately: on the machine these were measured on, six concurrent sessions inflate a cold check by ~1.8x with nothing about the tree changed (TreeOps 45s to 77s, JsonParse 52s to 99s within one three-run leg), so a budget seeded from the median would fire on a busy afternoon and teach a reader to ignore it. The 20s floor is for the sub-5s modules, where 2x is inside ordinary process-start noise. These are figures from a Windows dev machine; CI's windows-latest runner is a different machine and its first runs are what will say whether the tolerance is generous enough there. If it is not, that is a bump, and a bump is recorded.

modules.note: The first model, and the one section 11's delta recovery lives in. It carries no `--ext context_pruning`; what it carries instead is the SMT-pattern lesson (see the README's per-module costs) — `rev` / `app` / `ids_of` / `ops_of` rewrite into one another and their lemmas deliberately have NO `SMTPat`. Adding one back is the cost cliff here, and it is a cliff rather than a slope: the query stops returning.
The decode combinators. Default context, no scoped options; the cost is ordinary and the spread between an idle and a contended machine (15s to 33s) is most of it.

Carries `#set-options "--ext context_pruning"` near the top — 300s with the default context against 56s pruned, measured on the pinned prover. The single most expensive module in the leg even so, because it is an order of magnitude larger than DagFold. If this budget is ever bumped, check first that the pruning option is still in force: losing it is a 5x regression that looks like ordinary growth in the log. BUMPED by fuaran-core#162 from 160s/77s: sections 19 and 20 added the preorder-position lemma and the batch lift, some five hundred lines, and the lift is a mutual induction over the operation type and over lists of it — the shape that costs, because every case of it meets the module's whole membership algebra. Seeded over FIVE cold runs measuring 92s, 99s, 75s, 88s and 145s, and the number is 2x the 99s rather than 2x the 145s — which is a departure from the rule as written, so here is the reason rather than a silent choice. The 145s run inflated three UNTOUCHED modules by the same factor in the same pass (DagFold 58s against 35-49s, JsonParse 164s against 86-132s, Chain 31s against 16-23s), so it measures the afternoon and not this module; 2x145 would be 290s, a ceiling nothing on this machine could ever reach, and a detector that cannot fire is not one. 200s covers the worst run observed with room and still fires on a real regression. No COST finding fired at the OLD number on any of the five, which is the point of re-seeding here rather than waiting: the budget had been left behind by the module underneath it, and the first run to say so would have been someone else's contended afternoon.

The composite, thin on purpose — the argument is in the two halves it joins. At the 20s floor: 2x of a 2s measurement is inside process-start noise, so the floor is what keeps this entry from being a false-alarm generator.
The two integrity walkers. Default context; 2x of 12s rounds to the floor's neighbourhood anyway.

Carries `#set-options "--ext context_pruning"` at line 98 — 128s default against 72s pruned. The widest spread in the leg (52s to 99s across one three-run pass), because a 45-constructor alphabet in a large mutual group is exactly the shape a loaded machine punishes; the budget is sized for the top of that spread and not its middle.

The apply engine, seeded by the phase that added the model over SIX cold runs, two `-Runs 3` passes: 39s, 36s, 27s and then 25s, 42s, 32s. The slowest is the 42s, and it is the one the rule takes — it was measured with a sibling session's full repo gate running beside it on the same machine, which is precisely the contention the tolerance exists to absorb rather than a run to discard. 2x42 rounds to 90s. Seeding from the first pass alone would have given 80s, which every run still fits; the number moved because the rule says slowest observed, and a rule applied only to the convenient half of the data is not the rule. Carries `#set-options "--ext context_pruning"` like the two modules above, and one SCOPED exception beside it that this budget depends on: `invert_applicable` proves 78 goals in a single query and sits under `#push-options "--z3rlimit 200"`, because at the leg's default 40 it was close enough to the ceiling that a different `--quake` seed exhausted it — green standalone, red under check.ps1. If this module ever needs a large bump, check that BOTH are still in force before believing the growth is ordinary: losing the scoped rlimit does not read as slowness, it reads as a flake. BUMPED by fuaran-core#140 from 90s/42s: section 8 added the container capability — a second engine clause for clause, the invariant, two premise refutations and the `--quake`-proved lemmas over them. Seeded from a `-Runs 3` pass measuring 85s, 93s and 65s, so the rule's SLOWEST observed is the 93s and 2x93 rounds to 190. Two things about that are worth the sentence. The first draft of this bump used the 71s a single earlier run had measured and set 150s — which is the rule applied to the convenient half of the data, exactly what the seeding note above warns against, and the 93s run happened in the very pass that would have shipped it. The second is that the 93s run EXCEEDED the old 90s budget: this is not a ceiling raised to fit a green run, it is a budget that had genuinely been left behind by the module underneath it.

The diff — `Diff.toOps`'s two refusals, the four passes, and the container-aware mirror. Seeded over EIGHT cold runs: 9s, 10s, 9s, 9s, 9s before the Phase 161 merge and 12s, 9s, 9s after it, so the rule's slowest observed is 12s, 2x is 24s and the next 10s is 30. It was first written as the 20s floor off the first five runs, and the 12s arrived in the very pass that would have shipped that number — the same shape `Preservation`'s entry below records, and the reason the rule says slowest rather than typical. Nothing regressed: the 12s run is inside the old 20s too, and the module is unchanged between the two passes; what moved is which runs the rule had seen. It is the cheapest model in the leg after `Skeleton`, and the reason is worth knowing before anyone reads a future bump as ordinary growth: what is proved here is what the four passes GUARANTEE ABOUT THE SCRIPT — shape, order and the refusal characterisation — and not what applying that script DOES, which the README's theorem 6 carries at level 2 instead. The lemmas are therefore structural inductions over lists, which Z3 discharges quickly; the reconstruction theorem, if it is ever taken, reasons about `ins` and `rem_at` over intermediate trees and would put this module in `Preservation`'s cost class rather than `Chain`'s. Carries `#set-options "--ext context_pruning"`, like the three modules above and for the same reason — it opens `TreeOps` and `DagFold`, whose ninety-odd patterned lemmas would otherwise be live at every query here. BUMPED by fuaran-core#162 from 30s/12s: section 9 added the positional facts over the preorder-position lemma, which are the module's first inductions over the TREE rather than over a list — the prediction in the sentence above, arriving for the positional half and not for the reconstruction half. Seeded over FOUR cold runs measuring 13s, 21s, 13s and 37s: the rule's slowest observed is the 37s, 2x37 is 74 and the next 10s is 80. Where that 37s came from is worth knowing before anyone reads a future figure as ordinary growth — it was measured in a pass that spiked machine-wide, with `JsonParse` at 132s against its usual 86-105 and `Preservation` at 127s against its usual 57-65 in the same run, on a machine carrying six concurrent proof sessions. The rule takes the slowest observed anyway, deliberately and for the reason its own note gives; recording the provenance is how the next reader tells a slow afternoon from a regression.
